newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Nemtsov-Russia could increase control over UES.
newsitem.headline: Nemtsov-Russia could increase control over UES.

text.p: Russian First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov, in charge of natural monopoly reform, said on Tuesday that the government could increase control over Unified Energy System (UES) national power utility.
"Government control may be increased, as the company is a natural monopoly from the point of view of energy and transport," he told a news conference.
Russia describes its state-controlled electricity, gas and railway networks as natural monopolies.
Nemtsov also said that the Central Dispatching Unit, which controls the movement of power on the national grid which UES owns, would remain part of the company.

Nemtsov said after a meeting on reforming UES that government representatives on the board of directors of UES, of which Russia has about 52 percent, would meet separately in order to present a unified government position to the company.
"It is necessary to bring a consolidated government position to the company," he said.
Nemtsov also said the presidency and chairmanship of the company, both currently held by Anatoly Dyakov, would be split.
The government has previously recommended Fuel and Energy Minister Pyotr Rodionov, who has since tendered his resignation, as UES chairman.
But Nemtsov did not say whether Rodionov was still under consideration and Rodionov told Reuters that his nomination could be rescinded given his resignation.

Nemtsov, appointed to a top position in Russia's new reformist cabinet to restructure natural monopolies, said closed-doors meetings to award contracts, including to foreigners, had to be stopped, investor rights respected and an independent auditor appointed.

UES, which is Russia's largest company by sales and staff and one of its biggest by market capitalisation, controls the national power grid and wholesale market, has majority stakes in most local power utilities and owns generating plants.
Nemtsov said UES's power generation capability would have to be given free access to the energy market.
But he said the Central Dispatching Unit, which critics say need to be cut off from the rest of the company to achieve a fair market, should stay in the company.
